title: Up All Night

jokes.text: They're very expensive freshwater clams from the... Cuyahoga River.
jokes.setup: Jack defends the seafood that gave everyone food poisoning, calling it expensive and high-quality
jokes.punchline: The source is the notoriously polluted Cuyahoga River in Cleveland — famous for having literally caught fire
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack obliviousness delivered deadpan. The Cuyahoga River is a perfect specific detail — it's the river that famously caught fire in 1969, making it a shorthand for pollution. Jack's confidence while naming the worst possible clam source is pure character comedy and lands hard. The pause before 'Cuyahoga River' suggests even Jack knows how bad this sounds but won't concede the point.

jokes.text: My whole staff has been blorching for three days
jokes.setup: Liz is explaining the severity of the food poisoning
jokes.punchline: 'Blorching' — a made-up word that perfectly evokes violent illness without spelling it out, delivered casually as if it's a real word
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's habit of inventing disgusting-sounding portmanteaus pays off here. 'Blorching' sounds exactly like what it describes. The casualness of its delivery — as if everyone knows what it means — is part of the joke. It's economical and memorable.

jokes.text: making love on the floor of the Concorde. Then the next, your lawyers are fighting over who gets to keep the box your dog defecates in.
jokes.setup: Jack is describing how quickly marriage can turn sour
jokes.punchline: The contrast drops from glamorous mile-high-club sex on a supersonic jet to fighting over a dog's litter box — the specific absurdity of coveting the defecation box is the topper
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural joke. The Concorde-to-defecation-box contrast is perfectly calibrated — both details are specific and both are distinctly Jack's world (only Jack would have sex on a Concorde; only a wealthy divorce would contest ownership of the dog box). The structure earns an 8+ because it's not just high/low contrast — it's that the low thing is still somehow a luxury item (a specific, fought-over box). Pure character integration.

jokes.text: You taught your dog to poop in a box? / Bianca did. But I want that box.
jokes.setup: Liz takes the mundane surface question — who taught the dog to use a box
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately corrects the attribution and then firmly asserts his ownership claim over a dog toilet
jokes.explanation: A crisp callback that deepens the previous joke. The economy is nearly perfect — four words ('But I want that box') do enormous work to characterize Jack's petty, competitive need to win. The laugh comes from his total commitment to a profoundly undignified position.

jokes.text: Are you angry or excited right now? I can't tell.
jokes.setup: Jack describes fighting, conniving, and clawing with Bianca — language equally suited to combat or passion
jokes.punchline: Liz calls out the ambiguity directly, suggesting Jack can't distinguish between hatred and desire for Bianca
jokes.explanation: A well-timed observational punchline from Liz that crystallizes the Jack/Bianca dynamic that drives the whole episode. The economy is excellent — the ambiguity is real and the joke earns it rather than forcing it.

jokes.text: This would work on 'Ugly Betty.'
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably a writer or Jack) witnesses Bianca's entrance and comments on its dramatic quality
jokes.punchline: Meta-dismissal: calling out that the moment is telenovela-level melodrama that would only work on a competing ABC show, not on 30 Rock
jokes.explanation: Sharp meta-joke that doubles as a network rivalry dig. 'Ugly Betty' was airing simultaneously on ABC and trafficked in exactly this kind of romantic drama. The self-awareness of calling out a competitor while acknowledging 30 Rock wouldn't play it straight is clever and economical.

jokes.text: Me and Angie rented the penthouse at the Soho Grand, where we will drink wine and pleasure each other.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains his Valentine's plans
jokes.punchline: The blunt clinical phrasing 'pleasure each other' delivered with total sincerity is Tracy's voice exactly — simultaneously over-sharing and strangely formal
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy voice — the formal clinical construction of 'pleasure each other' is funnier than any crude phrasing would be. His sincerity makes it work.

jokes.text: That's why me and my wife role-play. She put on a girl scout outfit with a box of cookies, and I answer the door in my boxers. Or I rent out a wheelchair, and she pretends to be my caseworker.
jokes.setup: Pete agrees you have to keep things spicy after 17 years of marriage
jokes.punchline: The role-play scenarios escalate from a mildly naughty fantasy to a wheelchair/caseworker scenario that implies Pete feels dependent and helpless in his marriage — darkly self-revealing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from girl-scout-cookies fantasy to wheelchair-caseworker role-play is perfect — the second scenario reveals Pete's sad marriage dynamic under the guise of sexy role-play. 'And in a way, she is' is the devastating topper. Textbook escalation with genuine character depth. Justifies the 8+ score by being both funny and illuminating about Pete's emasculation.

jokes.text: And, in a way, she is.
jokes.setup: Pete describes his wife role-playing as his caseworker
jokes.punchline: Pete adds the devastating aside that she functionally is his caseworker — she manages his life
jokes.explanation: This five-word button is the best single unit of comedy in the episode. Perfect economy — it needs no elaboration. The joke is that Pete said it meaning it as a sexy fantasy, then in real time accepted the literal truth of it. It's self-aware, character-specific, dark, and structurally immaculate. Earns the 8.8 craft score by functioning simultaneously as punchline AND character revelation AND darkly funny acceptance. Comparable to the calibration anchor standard.

jokes.text: I just took a whole bunch of Cialis, because I have big Valentine's plans tonight. / With who? / Uh, nobody.
jokes.setup: Lutz announces he took erectile dysfunction medication for Valentine's Day plans
jokes.punchline: He has no actual plans — he took Cialis for no one
jokes.explanation: Simple but effective cringe joke. The beat between 'With who?' and 'Uh, nobody' is perfectly timed. Lutz's haplessness is well-deployed and the specificity of Cialis (not a vague reference) sharpens it.

jokes.text: He keeps sending me all these flowers to apologize, but he's still insisting on having a Greek Orthodox wedding. But I really disagree with the church's stance on Cyprus.
jokes.setup: Cerie is explaining why she and her fiancé are fighting on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The geopolitical objection to the Greek Orthodox church's position on the Cyprus dispute is a deeply specific, extremely unexpected source of marital tension from a character portrayed as shallow
jokes.explanation: A brilliant subversion of Cerie's established airhead persona. The Cyprus geopolitical conflict is such a precise, real, and obscure objection that it gets a huge laugh from the surprise alone. It's the opposite of what we expect from Cerie and suggests hidden depths (or absurd randomness — either reading is funny). Earns 8+ for originality and the sophistication of the character subversion.

jokes.text: I want the art supplies that I gave you on your 40th birthday and any subsequent art projects you made with them.
jokes.setup: Jack is listing demands in the divorce settlement — jewelry, art supplies are being itemized
jokes.punchline: The reach to claim ownership of all art SHE made WITH his supplies is absurdly controlling and petty — and distinctly Jack
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of divorce demands is well-constructed. Each item gets more ridiculous. Claiming the art projects she made with his gift supplies is the right kind of petty genius that defines Jack's competitive nature.

jokes.text: I want all of your parents' love letters.
jokes.setup: The divorce demand list escalates — their love letters feel reasonable, then Jack demands HER PARENTS' love letters
jokes.punchline: Claiming intimate correspondence between Bianca's parents is a genuinely shocking escalation that has nothing to do with marital assets
jokes.explanation: The best beat in the divorce demands escalation. The jump from 'our love letters' to 'your parents' love letters' is a perfect comedic leap — it has a clear internal logic (Jack wants anything intimate that belongs to Bianca) while being completely insane. The brevity is key. Earns 8+ because it's a genuinely surprising escalation that also reveals the depth of Jack's possessiveness and cruelty.

jokes.text: Oh, damn it, Johnny! You know I love my Big Beef and Cheddar!
jokes.setup: The divorce demands have been solemn (jewelry, art, love letters); Jack demands the Arby's franchise
jokes.punchline: Bianca, who has coolly agreed to every demand including love letters and art, finally breaks over an Arby's sandwich item — revealing an unexpected, very human attachment
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection and character reveal. After serenely relinquishing jewelry, art, and love letters, Bianca loses composure over a fast-food menu item. It's funny because it's specific (Big Beef and Cheddar, not 'Arby's food'), because it humanizes a glamorous character, and because it's the exact kind of thing that would actually matter. Quotable and memorable.

jokes.text: Break out a bottle of champagne. But not the one that came with the shellfish, okay? Some other bottle of champagne.
jokes.setup: Jack is celebrating his divorce being nearly final
jokes.punchline: He specifically excludes the poisoned shellfish champagne — a callback to the food poisoning cold open, delivered with Jack's characteristic fastidiousness
jokes.explanation: A clean callback that rewards attentive viewers. The repetition of 'some other bottle of champagne' is slightly over-explained but still lands. Jack's matter-of-fact awareness that the champagne was contaminated without any remorse is on-brand.

jokes.text: It's also her birthday.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'who cares, it's just Valentine's Day' to comfort Pete about missing his wife's Valentine's
jokes.punchline: It's also her birthday — making Pete's failure catastrophically worse
jokes.explanation: The comedic economy here is near-perfect — four words that demolish Liz's reassurance and massively escalate Pete's situation. The concept isn't novel but the timing and compression are excellent. Gets a reaction because it's so perfectly structured.

jokes.text: Did you just come from a Suzanne Somers look-alike contest?
jokes.setup: Jenna enters in an unusual outfit
jokes.punchline: Frank's backhanded compliment/insult equating Jenna's look to Suzanne Somers (dated, aging sex symbol) is cutting and specific
jokes.explanation: Competent insult joke with a specific target. Suzanne Somers is a well-chosen reference for Jenna's type of aging blonde celebrity. Not exceptional but lands solidly.

jokes.text: Vagina Day is a charity event founded by a group of celebrities who have, for whatever reason, never been asked to participate in 'The Vagina Monologues.'
jokes.setup: 'Is that an offshoot of The Vagina Monologues?'
jokes.punchline: The founding premise — celebrities specifically excluded from a prestigious vagina-related event — is both absurd and wickedly specific about Hollywood social hierarchies
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke construction. The 'for whatever reason' parenthetical is key — it implies Jenna doesn't acknowledge why she wasn't invited, and that the reason is obvious. It's also a sharp satire of celebrity charity culture and the prestige economy of progressive causes. Character-specific: only Jenna's combination of narcissism and obliviousness makes this work.

jokes.text: My vagina is a flower. A weird, ugly flower.
jokes.setup: Jenna is defending the legitimacy of Vagina Day performances
jokes.punchline: She delivers a sample monologue — the self-deprecating modifier 'weird, ugly' undercuts what should be a poetic affirmation
jokes.explanation: The self-sabotaging structure of the monologue is funny — it starts as clichéd poetry and then Jenna undermines it herself. Memorable and quotable. The joke works because Jenna both takes it seriously and doesn't realize she's insulting herself.

jokes.text: I remember the night I lost my virginity. It was 1968, during the Democratic convention.
jokes.setup: Jenna continues her Vagina Day monologue sample
jokes.punchline: The Chicago Democratic Convention of 1968 was one of the most violent, chaotic political events in American history — an unexpected and disturbing context for losing one's virginity
jokes.explanation: A beautifully specific historical detail that creates dark comedy through juxtaposition. It also implies Jenna is significantly older than she lets on (she'd have to be at least 16 in 1968 to make this work, making her at least 55 in 2007). The specificity of '1968 Democratic convention' is what elevates this above a generic 'I'm old' joke.

jokes.text: I'm divorced, everyone! Who wants to grab a drink?
jokes.setup: Jack has just received news that his divorce is final
jokes.punchline: Jack bursts into the writers' room announcing his divorce to strangers and immediately pivoting to celebrating — treating personal crisis as a networking opportunity
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Jack's emotional regulation problem expressed through social performance. The writers' room's awkward non-response is the real joke.

jokes.text: Sorry. I got to duck out. I just found a Hallmark store open 70 blocks from here.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Pete for a drink; Pete excuses himself
jokes.punchline: The 70-block detail is the joke — Pete is so desperate to fix his Valentine's/birthday failure that he's located a card store three miles away in Manhattan and is running there
jokes.explanation: Good running gag beat. The specificity of '70 blocks' is funnier than a vague 'far away' — it implies Pete has researched every Hallmark in New York. Pays off the earlier setup efficiently.

jokes.text: Just one quick one. / I got to be downtown dressed as a ninja by 10:00.
jokes.setup: Jack convinces Tracy to have just one drink instead of going home to Angie
jokes.punchline: Tracy has a completely unexplained requirement to be dressed as a ninja downtown at 10pm — stated with full seriousness, never elaborated
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock absurdism — Tracy has a ninja appointment. No explanation is given or needed. The joke is funnier for being stated flatly as a logistical constraint rather than a punchline. The economy is excellent; the audience is trusted to find it funny without underlining.

jokes.text: Marry, boff, kill — Beyoncé, Paula Abdul, and Oprah. / Dude, that's beyond easy. Boff Beyoncé, kill Paula, marry Oprah.
jokes.setup: The writers kill time playing 'Marry, Boff, Kill'
jokes.punchline: The answer is delivered as completely obvious ('beyond easy') — the willingness to kill Paula Abdul and the confidence in marrying Oprah as a pragmatic choice says everything about the writers' room culture
jokes.explanation: The 'Marry Oprah' answer is the joke — it's a billionaire calculation that's both savvy and funny. Competent but not exceptional use of the MBK game format.

jokes.text: Marry, boff, kill — Cerie, Liz, and Jenna. / Marry Liz, get with Cerie, kill Jenna. / I can hear you!
jokes.setup: The game continues with present colleagues as subjects
jokes.punchline: Jenna objects not to being killed, or to anything else — she's simply announcing she can hear them, which makes everyone more uncomfortable, and we wait to see what she'll say about being chosen for 'kill'
jokes.explanation: The running gag with 'I can hear you' is well-timed cringe. The real laugh is that everyone knew she was there and played anyway. Sets up the Frank/Jenna conflict that pays off later.

jokes.text: But thank you for saying that you would marry me.
jokes.setup: Liz told Frank to stop playing MBK about people in the room
jokes.punchline: She quietly thanks him for choosing 'marry' for her — revealing she's more pleased about this than she'll admit
jokes.explanation: Excellent Liz Lemon character beat. The vulnerability underneath the bluster is perfect — she told everyone to stop but couldn't resist accepting the compliment. 'Thank you for saying that you would marry me' is a beautifully awkward construction. Very Liz.

jokes.text: No, I'm not with so many men that it's impossible for me to guess.
jokes.setup: Liz is on the phone with the florist trying to identify who sent her flowers; the florist apparently suggests it could be any of many men
jokes.punchline: We only hear Liz's side — but her denial ('I'm not with so many men') is funny because it's so defensive and because the florist clearly hit a nerve. The denial suggests more defensiveness than the accusation warranted.
jokes.explanation: Good one-sided phone call joke. The technique of only hearing Liz's side lets viewers fill in a more insulting version of the florist's question. Her protesting-too-much denial is perfectly Liz.

jokes.text: Oh. Oh, well, you know what? I found the card, actually. They're from your mom. Yeah. So tell your gay mom I said thanks.
jokes.setup: Liz is flustered and losing the argument with the florist on the phone
jokes.punchline: She fabricates a solution and pivots to a petty 'your mom' insult at a florist who isn't even in the room — the specificity of 'gay mom' is the topper
jokes.explanation: Liz's social awkwardness and combativeness collide in a funny way. The 'your mom' escalation with 'gay' modifier is juvenile in a way that feels earned for Liz — she's a 30-something woman hurling playground insults at a stranger. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: We got to order some more champagne, go and jump on my helicopter and buzz Trump Tower until Don comes out on the roof and begs us to stop.
jokes.setup: Jack is planning his divorce celebration activities
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'buzzing Trump Tower until Don comes out on the roof' as a celebration activity is absurd in exactly the right way — it's petty, wealthy, and involves a real person in an embarrassing scenario
jokes.explanation: This joke has aged interestingly — a 2007 reference to helicoptering Trump Tower to annoy Donald Trump. Jack's elite mischief plan is perfectly calibrated: only someone with a helicopter and connections to Trump would plan this as casual fun. Strong character specificity.

jokes.text: That is the weak married man inside you talking. I used to be like you. Always remember — marriage is a competition. And after 18 years of overtime, I am finally going to claim victory.
jokes.setup: Tracy says he needs to call his wife to say he'll be late
jokes.punchline: Jack reframes Tracy's marital fidelity as weakness and his own divorce as 'victory' — the sports metaphor for a failed marriage is darkly funny
jokes.explanation: The 'victory' framing for a 18-year marriage ending in divorce is genuinely dark and funny. Jack's competitive nature corrupting his ability to process emotional situations is core character comedy.

jokes.text: Bone Osama bin Laden. To shame him. And then his own people would murder him.
jokes.setup: The MBK trio includes Osama bin Laden; participants need to assign actions
jokes.punchline: The reasoning — sleep with bin Laden to create a sex scandal that would get him killed by his followers — is a darkly elaborate and oddly logical counter-terrorism strategy
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Toofer has worked out the geopolitical logic — it's not just shock value, it's a complete strategic argument delivered in MBK context. The specificity of 'his own people would murder him' makes it land harder than a simpler answer would. Dark but constructed.

jokes.text: Marry Martha Stewart. 'Cause, you know, she seems like a dirty bird.
jokes.setup: Toofer assigning MBK actions to Martha Stewart
jokes.punchline: 'Dirty bird' applied to Martha Stewart — the ultimate domestic propriety icon — is a perfect inversion
jokes.explanation: The subversion of Martha Stewart's prim image with 'dirty bird' is economical and well-targeted. The 'you know' hedging makes it funnier — as if it's common knowledge.

jokes.text: I'd marry Toofer 'cause he's classy. I'd kill Lutz. Sorry, Lutz. The thought that you would do anything to me is awesome. And I'd boff Kenneth.
jokes.setup: Cerie is given a MBK trio of her male colleagues
jokes.punchline: Cerie would kill Lutz without hesitation (then apologizes), finds the idea of Lutz doing anything to her 'awesome' in the most condescending way, and then chooses Kenneth — shocking Kenneth himself
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble beat. The 'Sorry, Lutz' / 'awesome' combo is the strongest part — Lutz accepts his fate stoically and Cerie's condescension is pitch-perfect. Kenneth's 'What?! Really?' sets up the Frank/Jenna subplot.

jokes.text: And does a phony bare her soul for the homeless? Because that comes from in here. My vagina is a convenience store... clean and reliable and closed on Christmas.
jokes.setup: Frank calls Jenna a phony; she defends herself by returning to her Vagina Day material
jokes.punchline: The convenience store metaphor for her vagina — 'clean and reliable and closed on Christmas' — is bizarrely specific and self-undermining while Jenna thinks it's profound
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The convenience store metaphor is inspired — it's mundane, oddly specific, and the 'closed on Christmas' detail is perfect both as a mundane business fact and as an accidental piece of autobiography. Jenna delivers it as earnest soul-baring, which makes it land harder. 'Clean and reliable' describing Jenna's sex life is also darkly funny given her character. Highly quotable. Earns the 8+ score for originality and structural perfection of the metaphor.

jokes.text: Fake. And weird.
jokes.setup: Jenna has just delivered the 'convenience store' vagina monologue as proof of her authenticity
jokes.punchline: Frank's two-word dismissal after the elaborate monologue — 'Fake. And weird.' — is the most economic possible response
jokes.explanation: The economy is perfect — Frank refuses to engage with the monologue on its own terms and dismisses it in four syllables. Works as a punctuation mark on Jenna's elaborate speech.

jokes.text: Frank's button: 'Fake. And weird.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has just delivered the convenience store vagina monologue as proof of her authenticity.
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses it in two words: 'Fake. And weird.'
jokes.explanation: The button to Jenna's monologue. Four syllables that completely deflate the preceding absurdity. The economy is perfect — he needed exactly two words. The rhythm ('Fake.' pause 'And weird.') suggests Frank didn't even have to think about it, which is funnier than a longer dismissal.

jokes.text: She is the succubus from the bowels of hell. I mean, if I were forced to remember her as I first met her... then, yes, empirically, she is very, very beautiful. But it's what's inside her that really makes her disgusting.
jokes.setup: Jack is toasting to his freedom from Bianca, cataloguing her awfulness
jokes.punchline: The qualification 'empirically' — and the slow concession that she's beautiful — before the twist that it's her INTERIOR that's disgusting, which he says right after longing for her, undercuts his entire speech
jokes.explanation: The speech is a good slow-build that reveals Jack's inability to actually let go of Bianca. 'Empirically' is a perfect Jack word — he can't even acknowledge her beauty without qualifying it scientifically. The structure of the speech works as escalating self-contradiction.

jokes.text: I wish I could touch her boobs again. She really had a fabulous pair of boobs.
jokes.setup: Jack has been building an elaborate case for why Bianca is terrible
jokes.punchline: He breaks completely from the speech to deliver this aside with total sincerity, then doubles down with 'fabulous'
jokes.explanation: The tonal rupture from 'succubus from the bowels of hell' to 'fabulous pair of boobs' is well-executed. It's the most honest thing Jack says all episode and the sincerity makes it funnier. His word choice ('fabulous') is characteristically Jack — even his lustful asides have a certain formality.

jokes.text: I admit sometimes I would fantasize about her getting various terminal illnesses, and I would nurse her... to her death. And she would say, 'Johnny, I am in so much pain.' And I would say, 'Just hang in there a little longer, Bianca.'
jokes.setup: Jack continues his rambling, wine-fueled toast about Bianca
jokes.punchline: His romantic fantasy is a prolonged deathbed nursing scenario where he slowly lets her die — presented as a love story
jokes.explanation: One of the darkest and most brilliant jokes in the episode. Jack's 'fantasy' of nursing Bianca through terminal illness while stringing out her death ('just hang in there a little longer') is a perfect expression of his love/hatred — he wants her near and suffering, which is actually very specific. The dialogue he imagines is chillingly tender. Near-perfectly calibrated dark comedy. Earns the 8.5+ because it's character-specific (only Jack would romanticize this), structurally complete (setup/payoff within the monologue), and genuinely surprising in its darkness.

jokes.text: Jack's pivot at the end of his 'love' speech: '...what are you doing tonight?'
jokes.setup: Jack has delivered a beautiful, sincere speech about love and finding happiness again.
jokes.punchline: He turns directly to Tracy and asks 'what are you doing tonight?' — a non-sequitur that either means he's asking Tracy on a date or he's so lonely after the speech he immediately needs company.
jokes.explanation: The abrupt pivot from profound romantic declaration to 'what are you doing tonight?' is a classic 30 Rock deflation. Jack's entire speech about finding love again resolves in him asking Tracy Jordan to hang out on Valentine's night — which perfectly captures both Jack's emotional vulnerability AND the absurdity of his current situation. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Kenneth, this is your chance. Cerie digs you. / Cerie said she would do it with you. / Well, that just makes me perspire.
jokes.setup: Frank and Toofer tell Kenneth that Cerie chose him in MBK and encourage him to make a move
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response — 'that just makes me perspire' — is the most Kenneth possible expression of arousal, using a word that implies anxiety and physical discomfort rather than excitement
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's 'perspire' response is excellent character writing. 'Perspire' is such a specific, formal, slightly Victorian word choice that it perfectly captures Kenneth's Southern gentility colliding with an unexpected sexual situation. It's funny, pure character, and efficient. Earns the 8.0 for character integration alone — this line could only be Kenneth's.

jokes.text: Pete role-playing as a maintenance worker to sneak into his wife's hotel room — 'I'm detecting a lot of heat over here... I think it's coming... from my butt.'
jokes.setup: Pete has disguised himself as a maintenance worker to surprise his wife for Valentine's/birthday; he's doing a fake 'nitrogen leak' inspection
jokes.punchline: Pete breaks the professional pretense when, apparently, he actually passes gas — 'I think it's coming from my butt'
jokes.explanation: Pete's role-play setup failing via flatulence is consistent with his character's hapless marriage dynamic. Not especially original — the 'disguise ruined by accident' beats a familiar path — but the specific 'nitrogen leak' conceit and Pete's tragic commitment to romance sell it.

jokes.text: Oh, no! I'm married!
jokes.setup: Pete's wife realizes it's him through the disguise and the role-play shifts into something romantic/erotic
jokes.punchline: Pete yells 'I'm married!' — an odd thing to say to your own wife, implying either he's committed to the fiction of her being a stranger or he momentarily forgot the role-play
jokes.explanation: A very funny line with perfect economy. It's a callback to the role-play setup (she's pretending to be a stranger) but also has a meta-quality — Pete is too committed to the role, or too confused, to break character. 'I'm married!' as a line of erotic role-play is an inspired inversion. Strong laugh, highly quotable.

jokes.text: Okay, I don't know who that is. But we done, 'cause I'm not Velcro-ing up again.
jokes.setup: Tracy and others burst into Pete and Paula's hotel room mid-role-play
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not Velcro-ing up again' implies she had to Velcro something as part of the role-play outfit — unexplained detail that implies more elaborate costuming than shown
jokes.explanation: The Velcro detail is inspired — it implies the sex prop/outfit without showing anything, and 'I'm not Velcro-ing up again' has the weary tone of someone who had to work to get into costume. Economical and implies more than it shows.

jokes.text: Tracy bursts in: 'Happy Valentimes!'
jokes.setup: Tracy has shown up at Pete's hotel room with people in tow.
jokes.punchline: 'Valentimes' — Tracy consistently mispronounces Valentine's Day as 'Valentimes' throughout the episode.
jokes.explanation: This is the first instance of Tracy's 'Valentimes' running gag. The mispronunciation is character-specific (Tracy is not educated in conventional ways), delivered with total sincerity, and becomes a running joke that earns bigger laughs with each repetition. High quotability because it's the kind of thing people adopt in real life.

jokes.text: This is a Krug Clos du Mesnil, and I was saving it for a special occasion. And I thought to myself, 'My God. This is it.'
jokes.setup: Jack is sharing expensive champagne with the ragtag group in Pete's hotel room — Tracy, Angie, a stranger
jokes.punchline: Jack has reserved a presumably $500+ bottle of prestige champagne for this moment — stranded in a stranger's hotel room after being ejected from his own, surrounded by people he barely knows
jokes.explanation: Jack's ability to find any occasion worthy of his finest champagne is excellent character comedy. The dramatic 'My God. This is it.' delivered about an accidental hotel-room party with strangers is perfectly Jack-oblivious.

jokes.text: Isn't she precious? Hey, fun fact about Vlem. She originally came here to study engineering.
jokes.setup: Jack introduces the woman he apparently brought to the hotel — possibly a sex worker — and speaks about her reductively
jokes.punchline: 'Fun fact about Vlem' — introducing a person's resume mid-party as a deflection from the awkward context — implies she had ambitions that didn't pan out into something Jack would explain with 'fun fact'
jokes.explanation: The 'fun fact' framing for a sex worker's engineering background is darkly funny — Jack reduces her to a novelty data point while clearly having hired her for the evening. It's dark without being crude.

jokes.text: You tell G.E. light-bulb man, I want 'Sophie's Choice' out of my suite!
jokes.setup: Jack wants someone removed from his hotel suite
jokes.punchline: 'Sophie's Choice' as a shorthand for an impossible decision, but applied to a hotel eviction — and Jack referring to himself as 'G.E. light-bulb man' through a third party is an absurd self-reference
jokes.explanation: Slightly muddy but the 'G.E. light-bulb man' self-reference is a good detail — Jack describing himself through his corporate identity. 'Sophie's Choice' in this context is a bit forced.

jokes.text: In fact, she's pretty sure I'm the reincarnated soul of Adrian Twyfer. He was our town minister who died in an organ fire.
jokes.setup: Cerie says Kenneth is an 'old soul'; Kenneth explains his mother's belief about his origins
jokes.punchline: A town minister who 'died in an organ fire' — the specificity of the organ fire as cause of death is perfectly absurd, and the matter-of-fact delivery makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Died in an organ fire' is a perfect piece of 30 Rock absurdist specificity — it's a real instrument, a plausible if extraordinary death, and it comes from Kenneth's Southern small-town mythology. The delivery would be completely earnest. 'An organ fire' sounds almost too specific to be made up, which gives it a surreal quality. Earns the 8.5 for originality and economy — five words that are a complete, strange world.

jokes.text: Well, it's like Dr. Laura Schlessinger says. Women should be more accommodating to their men, for the health of the marriage. / She sounds smart. Is she really a doctor? / No, I think she's kind of like Dr Pepper.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is giving Cerie relationship advice and cites Dr. Laura
jokes.punchline: Cerie's earnest question 'Is she really a doctor?' followed by Kenneth's comparison to Dr Pepper — implying the 'Dr.' is a brand designation, not a credential
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The Dr Pepper analogy for Dr. Laura's credentials is a sharp, economical satirical point — and it comes from Kenneth, who genuinely admires Dr. Laura while also making this devastating critique without realizing it. Cerie's naivety ('Is she really a doctor?') sets up the punchline perfectly. The double character comedy (both Cerie and Kenneth being sincere) elevates it. Quotability is very high — 'kind of like Dr Pepper' is a perfect analogy that people will repeat.

jokes.text: Thanks, Kenneth. You give really good advice.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has just advised Cerie to be more accommodating and cited a radio host's dubious credentials
jokes.punchline: Cerie sincerely thanks Kenneth for advice that was fairly terrible — then immediately goes to meet her fiancé downtown, acting on it
jokes.explanation: A functional scene-closing beat but not a strong joke on its own. The comedy is in the gap between advice quality and Cerie's reception of it, but the punchline doesn't escalate beyond what we already understood.

jokes.text: Kenneth! / What? How dare you. / You're so weird. / Tell Liz I left, okay? And if you want to tell those guys upstairs that we made out, it's all right with me.
jokes.setup: Jenna apparently catches Kenneth doing something strange (implied by the immediate reaction 'How dare you')
jokes.punchline: Cerie, departing, casually tells Kenneth to spread the rumor that they made out — framing a lie as something she'd sanction, implying it helps her with something (the Frank/Jenna subplot)
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — Cerie gives Kenneth permission to lie about them making out, which is either an act of kindness toward Kenneth or self-interested manipulation. The ambiguity is funny. 'It's all right with me' is a great casual close.

jokes.text: This is the second-worst Valentine's Day we ever had.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Angie are stranded with Jack and strangers in a hotel room on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Angie's (or Tracy's) ranking of this as 'second-worst' implies they have a history of terrible Valentine's Days, and this one doesn't even top the list
jokes.explanation: The implied history of an even worse Valentine's Day is the joke. The ranking system suggests a detailed mental catalogue of bad romantic holidays. Economy is good — 'second-worst' does all the work.

jokes.text: Is Mr. Donaghy here? / Another prostitute?
jokes.setup: Someone comes to the hotel room door asking for Jack
jokes.punchline: Whoever answers has already encountered enough women looking for Jack that they assume this is another hired companion — 'another prostitute' implies multiple have arrived
jokes.explanation: The offhand 'another prostitute' is excellent — it implies this has happened before, tonight, which says more than any elaboration could. Two words of context do enormous comic work. Economy score near-perfect.

jokes.text: Liz opens the door: 'Another prostitute?'
jokes.setup: Someone knocks on Liz's door late at night.
jokes.punchline: Liz opens the door and her first words are 'Another prostitute?' — implying she's already received at least one that evening, delivered as casually as 'Another delivery?'
jokes.explanation: Two words that open a comedic void. The word 'Another' does all the work — it implies a running count, suggests earlier events we didn't see, and casually places prostitution as a mundane part of this evening. Delivered by Liz with zero alarm. Perfect economy (10/10): you cannot remove a single word from this joke. One of the episode's best line readings.

jokes.text: And I want Bianca to see that I'm moving on. / Well, then maybe you should call Bianca to help you carry your prostitute out of the hotel you were just ejected from.
jokes.setup: Jack explains he's celebrating to show Bianca he's moved on
jokes.punchline: Liz summarizes Jack's current actual situation — ejected from a hotel while managing a hired woman — which sharply contradicts his narrative of moving on
jokes.explanation: Good Liz-as-straight-man moment. Her recitation of Jack's actual circumstances is functionally a comedic list that exposes the gap between his self-image and reality. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Marry, boff, kill — Bianca. Which do you want to do? / All of them.
jokes.setup: Liz uses the MBK game structure to make Jack confront his feelings about Bianca
jokes.punchline: Jack answers 'all of them' — he wants to marry, sleep with, and kill Bianca simultaneously, which perfectly encapsulates their relationship
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The entire MBK running gag through the episode has been building to this perfect callback. Liz repurposing the game as a psychological diagnostic tool is brilliant, and Jack's one-word answer 'All of them' is both the funniest possible response and the most emotionally honest thing he says all episode. The economy is a 10 — three syllables resolve the entire Jack/Bianca arc while generating the biggest laugh. Perfectly earned, structurally masterful, completely character-specific. This is a 9+ caliber joke.

jokes.text: Uh, leave her there. It's nicer than where I found her.
jokes.setup: Jack needs to do something with the woman he brought to the hotel
jokes.punchline: His decision to leave her in the room — 'it's nicer than where I found her' — is both casually callous and implies she came from worse circumstances
jokes.explanation: Darkly funny Jack-ism. The utilitarian logic ('it's nicer than where I found her') is callous in a way that's characteristic of Jack's class obliviousness. Economical and bleak.

jokes.text: Admit it — you spend just as much time and energy trying to look weird as I do trying to look beautiful. And you can act like you hate me, but if I tried to kiss you right now, you would totally do it 'cause you're a big, phony jerk.
jokes.setup: Jenna turns Frank's 'phony' accusation back on him
jokes.punchline: Her argument that Frank's 'weird guy' aesthetic is as constructed as her 'sexy woman' aesthetic is actually a valid point, and she crowns it with a confident sexual threat/challenge
jokes.explanation: Jenna's counterattack has genuine wit. The observation about performative weirdness vs. performative beauty is an actual comic insight. The pivot to 'you would totally do it' is a confident, funny close. One of Jenna's better character moments.

jokes.text: Jenna confronts Frank: 'You wear your thrift-store T-shirts and your big, weird glasses... What does that even mean?' / Frank: 'It's pretty self-explanatory.' (about his 'Extra Cheese' hat)
jokes.setup: Jenna turns the 'fake' accusation back on Frank, pointing out his cultivated 'weird' aesthetic.
jokes.punchline: Frank's defense of his 'Extra Cheese' hat — 'It's pretty self-explanatory' — is both deadpan and slightly deranged. It is not self-explanatory.
jokes.explanation: Frank's unironic confidence about an objectively confusing hat is very in-character. Jenna's point that he's just as performatively fake as she is has genuine comic truth, and Frank's refusal to engage with the substance of the argument (just defending the hat) is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Okay, fine. I pooted. It's 3:00 in the morning. Are you happy? / Yeah, I'm happy, because that's the first time you've ever done something like a real person.
jokes.setup: Frank challenges Jenna to do something genuine; the scene has built toward a moment of authentic connection
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'genuine' act is admitting to flatulence — and Frank accepts it as true authenticity
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sweet and funny resolution. The joke works on two levels: Jenna finally doing something 'real' is the pettiest possible act, and Frank's sincere satisfaction with it is perfect character writing for him. 'Pooted' is also the right word choice — it's Jenna's register. The 3am detail contextualizes the worn-down honesty of the moment.

jokes.text: I could do it again. But I wouldn't want to show off.
jokes.setup: Frank says her authentic flatulence admission makes her seem like a real person
jokes.punchline: Jenna offers to repeat the feat but modestly restrains herself from 'showing off' — applying celebrity self-promotion logic to flatulence
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The modesty construction — 'I wouldn't want to show off' about flatulence — is perfectly Jenna. It applies her celebrity performance logic (managing public display, not overdoing it) to a bodily function. The economy is nearly perfect and the character integration is a 9 — only Jenna would say this, only in this context, and it crystallizes her entire personality. Comparable to the calibration anchor for 8+ scores.

jokes.text: Frank apologizes for saying he would kill Jenna. Jenna responds with sincere gratitude: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: The Frank/Jenna détente continues after the pooting breakthrough.
jokes.punchline: Frank apologizes for the Marry/Boff/Kill 'kill Jenna' vote. Jenna accepts his apology as though it's a normal social exchange — which normalizes the entire absurd game.
jokes.explanation: A functional callback that provides emotional resolution to the Frank/Jenna subplot while also being mildly absurd (apologizing for a hypothetical murder in a party game). Not a major laugh but a good grace note.

jokes.text: Way to go, loser. / Oh, yeah? If I blew it, then how did I get her underpants?
jokes.setup: The writers assume Kenneth struck out with Cerie; he's told he blew it
jokes.punchline: Kenneth produces Cerie's underwear as evidence of success — an utterly unexpected twist given Kenneth's purity and the scene we witnessed
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing punch for the Kenneth/Cerie subplot. The contrast between Kenneth's Southern gentleman innocence and the implication of this moment is perfect misdirection. We never find out how — and we don't need to. The gap between what we know of Kenneth and what this implies is the joke. Earns 8+ for structure and economy — the question itself ('how did I get her underpants?') is funnier than any answer could be.

jokes.text: It's almost like it never happened. / I wouldn't be surprised if that 5-inch scar across my abdomen was suddenly gone.
jokes.setup: Jack's lawyer says the divorce papers make it 'almost like it never happened'
jokes.punchline: Jack points out a physical scar — presumably from something Bianca did — that would need to disappear for that to be true
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark callback to the Jack/Bianca relationship mythology. A 5-inch scar 'across my abdomen' implies violence that we've never seen but completely believe in the context of their relationship. The specificity of '5-inch' makes it funnier than a vague scar reference. Jack's deadpan delivery ('I wouldn't be surprised if...') is perfect.

jokes.text: I'm gonna shut it down, leave it vacant, open the windows, and let nature have at it.
jokes.setup: Bianca asks Jack to promise not to sell the Arby's; Jack says he won't sell it
jokes.punchline: Jack's plan is not to sell it but to abandon it to nature — a 'scorched earth' strategy on a fast food franchise that is both petty and strangely poetic
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Jack move. He technically honors Bianca's request (he won't sell it) while doing the most destructive possible thing — 'let nature have at it' as a strategy for a retail property is absurdly specific and slightly poetic. It's the perfect Jack combination of following the letter of a promise while violating its spirit, wrapped in environmental rhetoric. Earns 8+ for originality and character integration — the phrasing 'let nature have at it' is Jack's specific brand of elevated pettiness.

jokes.text: Do it. / The case could be in court for months. / Maybe years. / Damn it, Johnny.
jokes.setup: Bianca threatens to take Jack to court over the Arby's abandonment; Jack dares her
jokes.punchline: Jack and the lawyer exchange competitive escalations ('months'/'years') as if extending the legal battle is attractive, and Bianca's resigned 'Damn it, Johnny' confirms she's been pulled back in
jokes.explanation: The perfect comedic resolution of the Jack/Bianca arc — they've manufactured a reason to stay entangled through the Arby's gambit. Jack's 'Do it' and then 'Maybe years' reveals he WANTS more legal proceedings as an excuse to stay connected to her. Bianca's 'Damn it, Johnny' is the romantic capitulation of the episode. The structure earns an 8+ for its elegant closure of the arc.

jokes.text: You know, I've heard that, in Greece, they have to change Charlton Heston's name on movie posters to Charlton Easton because in Greek the word 'heston' means 'to poop yourself.'
jokes.setup: Drew is trying to make conversation with Liz in her apartment; he spots a French Planet of the Apes poster
jokes.punchline: The 'heston means poop yourself in Greek' trivia is a completely made-up fact delivered with total confidence — funny for its specificity and the social awkwardness of leading with this information
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock fake trivia joke. The 'Charlton Easton / heston means poop yourself' bit is beautifully specific and delivered as an icebreaker by Drew, which characterizes him as charming-but-odd in a way that works for Liz. The specificity of 'Charlton Easton' as the replacement name makes it funnier than a vague claim.

jokes.text: You're a lawyer? / I prefer 'law stylist.'
jokes.setup: Liz establishes Drew works in Legal
jokes.punchline: 'Law stylist' — a made-up vanity title that applies the fashion industry's 'stylist' inflation to law, suggesting Drew is both self-important and playful
jokes.explanation: Economy is near-perfect — two words do the entire job. 'Law stylist' works because it's a real cultural phenomenon (job title inflation) applied to law. It characterizes Drew immediately as someone both competent and slightly ridiculous, which is the right note for a potential Liz love interest.

jokes.text: She pouted all night because she thought I forgot to send her something. You know, I told her I did, but she didn't believe me. / She sounds great.
jokes.setup: Drew explains his girlfriend Liz Lemler didn't believe he sent flowers despite his claim
jokes.punchline: Liz's dry 'She sounds great' — a sarcastic compliment about a suspicious, demanding girlfriend — is funny coming from Liz, who herself has trust issues and relational neuroses
jokes.explanation: Functional ironic payoff. Liz's 'She sounds great' is self-aware — she's essentially describing herself as insufferable, unknowingly. The irony works at two levels (sarcasm about the girlfriend + self-reflection) even if neither is explored.

jokes.text: But I could possibly get a photo of you with the flowers, like, with your I.D.
jokes.setup: Drew is trying to get the flowers back from Liz; she's resisting giving them up
jokes.punchline: He asks for a photo with her I.D. as 'proof' — a completely disproportionate, slightly invasive request that reveals either paranoia about his girlfriend or a lawyer's instinct to document everything
jokes.explanation: Good awkward comedy. The I.D. requirement is legally precise in a context where it's socially bizarre. Works as character comedy for Drew (law stylist habits) but doesn't fully land as a big joke.

jokes.text: Happy Valentimes! [third instance — Tracy to camera or passersby]
jokes.setup: Episode closing tag
jokes.punchline: The third and final 'Valentimes' closes the episode — the running gag gets its final beat, and it's funnier for being the closing word
jokes.explanation: The closing tag on a running gag always earns more than the individual instances. By the third 'Valentimes,' the audience has fully adopted it. Closing an episode on a character tic mispronunciation is economical and warm. High quotability — this is the line viewers leave the episode repeating.

tmdb_overview: It's Valentine's Day, and the TGS crew is celebrating by pulling an all nighter to put together a new episode. While Pete completely forgets the holiday, Kenneth and Cerie may be starting an office romance. Meanwhile, Liz wonders if Dennis is back in her life after she receives flowers from a secret admirer and newly divorced Jack wants to party with Tracy, who for once wants to spend a night alone with his wife instead.
insight: Season finale escalates absurdist chaos to 85.5, sustaining 2.59 jokes per minute.
